analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour over two years.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour died in a House subcommittee without a single cosponsor, a hearing, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage in two steps: to $5.65 an hour starting July 1, 2000, and to $6.15 an hour starting July 1, 2001 — a $1 increase from the current $5.15 [S2] [S3]. That is a raise of roughly 19% over two years for workers paid at or near the federal floor. It contained no tax offsets or carve-outs for employers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning at or near the $5.15 federal minimum wage, concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other service jobs. An estimated several million workers would see their hourly pay rise, first by 50 cents and then by another 50 cents. Workers earning slightly above the minimum could also see raises as pay scales adjusted upward. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour in the year beginning July 1, 2000, and to $6.15 an hour beginning July 1, 2001 — a straight $1 increase phased over two years with no phase-out, tax offset, or employer exemption in the bill.

The increase applies under the Fair Labor Standards Act's basic minimum wage provision (section 6(a)), which sets the floor for covered workers nationwide, so the raise reaches workers in every state rather than only states that set their own higher minimums.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers — chiefly restaurants, retail stores, and other low-wage service businesses — would pay higher hourly wages, and would typically cover some of that cost through small price increases. To the extent businesses adjusted, some entry-level positions or hours could be reduced. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The wage increase is a direct, unfunded cost increase for low-wage employers: the bill contains no tax credits or transition relief to offset the roughly $1-per-hour added labor cost for businesses that pay at the minimum.

The standard objection to any minimum wage increase is that higher mandated wages can lead some employers to cut hours, slow hiring, or raise prices — meaning some of the benefit to workers comes at a cost to entry-level job opportunities and to customers through slightly higher prices.

The two-step schedule starting July 1, 2000 meant the first increase would have taken effect barely three months after introduction, leaving employers little adjustment time compared with longer phase-ins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: a $1-an-hour raise — about $2,000 a year for a full-time minimum-wage worker — goes directly to the lowest-paid workers, who spend it immediately [S2] [S3]. The cost is higher payroll for low-wage employers and modestly higher prices, and some risk of reduced entry-level hiring. On balance, the transfer is large and targeted relative to a modest and diffuse cost, but the bill offered nothing to ease the transition for small businesses, which is likely why it drew no cosponsors even among wage-increase supporters, who had competing minimum wage bills in the same Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant introduced the Minimum Wage Act of 2000 in the House on April 4, 2000, to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour in two 50-cent steps.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which holds jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act.
On May 17, 2000, it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last action ever taken on the bill.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a subcommittee hearing, a committee markup, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses — avoided a $1-an-hour wage floor increase, while workers at the $5.15 minimum gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; minimum-wage workers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. James A. Traficant Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour over two years.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled; the bill was sent to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on May 17, 2000, and never moved again.

against.name: Rep. William F. Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action, leaving it to die in subcommittee.

against.name: House colleagues of Rep. Traficant
against.what_they_did: Not one member, from either party, signed on as a cosponsor of the bill during its eight-month life.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a partisan vote; the only measurable support was a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employer of minimum-wage workers, so a $1-an-hour wage floor increase would raise their labor costs directly. Their interest in blocking or diluting the increase ran against workers' interest in higher pay.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retail and service businesses paying near $5.15 an hour would have absorbed higher payroll costs, typically passed partly to customers through prices. The bill's death preserved the existing wage floor for them.
Not an industry, but the direct beneficiary group: workers at or near the minimum would have gained roughly $2,000 a year for full-time work, with a small risk of reduced entry-level hours.
